title: German Comfort or Italian Grip? How Lowa and Scarpa Boots Differ on Kenya's Mountains
meta_title: Lowa vs Scarpa: A Clear Boot Choice for 5 Kenyan Hikes
meta_description: Lowa vs Scarpa hiking boots compared on fit, weight, soles and durability, matched to five Kenyan hikes, plus what to check on a thrifted pair in Nairobi.
excerpt: Lowa vs Scarpa comes down to fit: Lowa for cushioning and wide-fit options on long, muddy days, Scarpa for a snug heel on scree, lava and rock in Kenya.
featured_image_alt: Lowa vs Scarpa hiking boots, three pairs of boots lined up against a stone wall
content:
Lowa vs Scarpa is less a question of quality than of how your heel and toes sit inside the boot. Lowa, from Bavaria, builds cushioned, roomier boots in several widths that feel comfortable early. Scarpa, from the foothills of the Italian Alps, builds snug, precise boots that grip the heel and suit rocky, steep ground.

Both names hang side by side on thrifted boot racks in Nairobi, so the choice comes up often. Below we compare the main models using each brand's own specifications, explain the fit and match them to Kenyan hikes, from Karura Forest to Point Lenana, so you can settle Lowa vs Scarpa before you pay.

Quick Facts

  • Origins: Lowa was founded in 1923 in Jetzendorf, Bavaria; Scarpa in 1938 in Asolo, in north-east Italy.
  • Day-hike flagships: the Lowa Renegade Evo GTX Mid (590 g per boot) and the Scarpa Terra GTX (615 g per boot, size 42).
  • Widths: Lowa sells the Renegade Evo in narrow, medium and wide; most Scarpa trekking boots come on a single medium last.
  • Waterproofing: GTX models from both brands use a GORE-TEX membrane, so neither has an edge in the short rains.
  • Lowa vs Scarpa in one line: Lowa for comfort on long, muddy days; Scarpa for a locked heel on scree, lava and rock.

Is Lowa or Scarpa Better for Hiking in Kenya?

Neither brand is better across the board. Lowa suits hikers who want cushioning, a choice of widths and a forgiving fit on long, muddy days. Scarpa suits hikers with narrow to average feet who want a firm heel hold on rock and loose ground. Fit decides the Lowa vs Scarpa question more than any label.

Kenyan trails test both. Black cotton mud on the Ngong Hills ridge in November rewards cushioning that does not rub over 11 km. The scree above Shipton's Camp on Mt Kenya, or Suswa's rough lava, rewards a boot that holds your heel still.

Renegade Evo GTX Mid vs Terra GTX: the day-hike pair

These two weigh almost the same, yet in a Lowa vs Scarpa try-on they feel quite different. Lowa's Renegade Evo GTX Mid page lists a double-injection PU midsole, a Monowrap frame that steadies the heel and two-zone lacing, so you can loosen the forefoot and lock the ankle separately.

Scarpa's Terra GTX page describes a thicker full-grain leather upper with a high cuff and a direct-attach PU midsole. That leather takes longer to soften but shrugs off thorny scrub at Hell's Gate. Some owners find its toe box slightly narrow, a point that often tips Lowa vs Scarpa for broad feet.

Camino and Tibet vs R-Evo, ZG and Mescalito: the trekking boots

For Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro, the Lowa vs Scarpa comparison moves up to stiffer boots. Lowa's Camino Evo GTX is the comfort choice for carrying 10-12 kg over four or five days, and the Tibet Evo GTX adds stiffness for scree and rock.

On the other side of the Lowa vs Scarpa line-up, three Scarpa boots share the job. The R-Evo GTX has a soft-shell Sock-Fit tongue that suits more foot shapes than most Italian boots. The ZG TRK GTX is lighter, and the Mescalito TRK GTX suits hikes that mix walking with scrambling.

How Do Lowa and Scarpa Boots Fit?

Lowa boots generally give more room around the toes and come in narrow, medium and wide versions of the Renegade. Scarpa boots usually hold the heel more tightly on a medium last. Whichever feels right first is usually the one to keep.

Lowa's size guide says to order your usual street-shoe size and try boots in the afternoon with hiking socks. Scarpa sizes in EU numbers, so a Lowa vs Scarpa size swap is rarely one-for-one; convert by foot length in centimetres instead. Our guide to hiking boot sizes in Kenya explains how UK, EU and US labels line up.

Lowa vs Scarpa for wide feet: which brand suits them?

Lowa usually suits wide feet better, because the Renegade Evo GTX Mid comes in a wide (E/EE) version as well as medium and narrow. Scarpa's standard trekking boots run medium, so broad-footed hikers should look for the wide version of a model, such as the ZG Trek Wide, or start with Lowa.

Do Lowa or Scarpa boots run small?

Neither brand runs badly small, but a thick sock changes the fit. With laces loose, you should slide a finger behind your heel. Longonot's stepped descent pushes toes forward, so leave a thumb's width in front of the longest toe. Thick merino wool hiking socks also fill small gaps.

Which Brand Lasts Longer on Kenyan Trails?

On durability, Lowa vs Scarpa is close: both outlast budget boots by years, thanks to polyurethane midsoles and Vibram rubber. Scarpa's resoleable ZG and Mescalito give it a small edge, while Lowa's Renegade keeps its shape over many seasons.

Red murram dust and black cotton mud are harder on leather than Alpine rain, because they dry it out. Wash them after each hike and dry them out of direct sun. Our hiking boot care routine covers cleaning and re-waterproofing, for both brands.

Lowa vs Scarpa by Trail: Matching the Boot to the Hike

Match the boot to the ground you walk most often, not the one big climb you might do.

  1. Karura Forest, Nairobi: firm, shaded paths. Any light boot works.
  2. Ngong Hills ridge, about 11 km: grassy climbs and sticky mud in the rains. The cushioned Lowa Renegade is the easier companion.
  3. Mt Longonot, 13.5 km circuit: loose ash and steep steps. Lowa vs Scarpa barely matters here; pick whichever holds your heel best.
  4. Elephant Hill and Table Mountain, Aberdares: bamboo, roots and bogs. Mid-height GTX boots from both brands, worn with gaiters.
  5. Mt Kenya to Point Lenana, 4,985 m: scree and frost on summit night. A Lowa Camino or Tibet, or a Scarpa R-Evo, ZG or Mescalito.

For the boggy Aberdares in November or April, water can pour over any collar, so add a pair of waterproof leg gaiters to whichever boot you choose.

Buying Lowa or Scarpa Second-Hand in Nairobi

A thrifted pair is the most affordable way into either brand in Kenya, because European leather boots have plenty of life left after one owner. In a Lowa vs Scarpa hunt on the rails, the checks match, with one extra for Scarpa: a stretched heel cup cancels its main strength.

Look at the tread first: Vibram lugs should still have clear edges. Press your thumb into the midsole; it should feel firm and springy, not brittle or crumbly. Check the GORE-TEX tag and size label inside the tongue, and flex the toe to look for cracks. Our longer checklist for second-hand hiking boots in Nairobi works for any Lowa vs Scarpa pair.

Pro Tips for Choosing Between the Two

  • Fit beats brand: settle Lowa vs Scarpa in the afternoon, wearing your hiking socks.
  • Test a slope: walk down stairs or a ramp; toes that hit the front mean the size or last is wrong.
  • Read the tongue: GTX means a GORE-TEX membrane; LL on a Lowa means a leather lining, better for dry, hot trails.
  • Mind the age: in any Lowa vs Scarpa bargain, a long-stored pair can hide a tired midsole.
  • Break them in: two or three Karura loops before any long climb.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Lowa vs Scarpa a big difference in comfort?

Comfort between the two brands differs mainly in feel. Lowa boots, especially the Renegade, feel cushioned almost from the first walk. Scarpa boots feel firmer and more precise, and their leather needs a few short hikes to soften. Hikers who want instant comfort tend to choose Lowa; fans of a locked heel on rough ground often choose Scarpa.

Are Scarpa boots narrower than Lowa?

Scarpa boots usually feel narrower than Lowa, mostly at the heel, because most Scarpa trekking boots use a single medium last with a snug heel cup. Lowa sells the Renegade Evo in narrow, medium and wide. Feet differ, so trying both on is the only sure test.

Lowa vs Scarpa for Mt Kenya: which should I pick?

Both brands make good Mt Kenya boots. A Lowa Camino Evo GTX or Tibet Evo GTX gives comfort and support under a loaded pack, while a Scarpa R-Evo, ZG TRK or Mescalito TRK gives a firm heel hold on the scree below Point Lenana. Choose the better-fitting pair and break it in before the climb.

Can you resole Lowa and Scarpa boots in Kenya?

Scarpa lists the ZG TRK GTX and Mescalito TRK GTX as resoleable at its approved repairers, and injected PU midsoles need specialist work. In Kenya, ask an experienced shoe repairer to look at the boot first, because not every repair shop can rebuild a trekking sole properly.

Where can I buy Lowa or Scarpa boots in Nairobi?

Both brands reach Nairobi mostly as thrifted stock. Our Mountain Mall shop on Thika Road lists Lowa pairs such as the Renegade Evo GTX Mid when they come in, and Scarpa pairs less often. WhatsApp us to ask what is in, or visit Shop D39 to try boots on.

Final Thoughts

Comfort first or grip first: that is the real split between these two boot makers. Lowa's cushioning and choice of widths make it the easier pick for long, muddy days near Nairobi, while Scarpa's snug heel pays off on scree, lava and steep rock. Lowa vs Scarpa gets simple once both are on your feet: bring your hiking socks, walk down a slope in each, and keep the pair that never lets your heel lift.
